Twin, one of the twelve (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18, etc.). He was also called Didymus (John 11:16; 20:24), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name.

Son of Simon (John 6:71; 13:2, 26), surnamed Iscariot, i.e., a man of Kerioth (Josh. 15:25). His name is uniformly the last in the list of the apostles, as given in the synoptic (i.e., the first three) Gospels.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ comforts his disciples (vv. 1–11); He further comforts his disciples (vv. 12–17); He still further comforts his disciples (vv. 18–31). People named: Philip, Thomas, Judas, Iscariot.
ch.mh: Here are three words, upon any of which stress may be laid.
q: Read verses 1–11 (Christ comforts his disciples). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 12–17 (He further comforts his disciples), what do you learn about family and generations?
Verse 6 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Acts 4:12. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Philip’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of love in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us rejoice in the Saviour's victories over Satan the prince of this world.
ch.a: Do one concrete, unannounced act of love for someone in your home or church.

bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ the true Vine (vv. 1–8); His love to his disciples (vv. 9–17); foretold (vv. 18–25); The Comforter promised (vv. 26,27).
ch.mh: Jesus Christ is the Vine, the true Vine.
q: Read verses 1–8 (Christ the true Vine). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–17 (His love to his disciples), what do you learn about love?
Verse 7 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 37:4. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: If the same power that first shed abroad the love of Christ's in our hearts, did not keep us in that love, we should not long abide in it.
ch.a: Do one concrete, unannounced act of love for someone in your home or church.

o: The promise of the Holy Spirit, and his office.
bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Persecution foretold (vv. 1–6); The promise of the Holy Spirit, and his office (vv. 7–15); Christ's departure and return (vv. 16–22); Encouragement to prayer (vv. 23–27); Christ's discoveries of himself (vv. 28–33).
ch.mh: Our Lord Jesus, by giving his disciples notice of trouble, designed that the terror might not be a surprise to them.
q: Read verses 1–6 (Persecution foretold). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 7–15 (The promise of the Holy Spirit, and his office), what do you learn about family and generations?
Verse 33 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside John 14:27. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of faith and trust in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We know not how we should act if brought into temptation; let us watch and pray without ceasing, that we may not be left to ourselves.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ's prayer for himself (vv. 1–5); His prayer for his disciples (vv. 6–10); His prayer (vv. 11–26).
ch.mh: Our Lord prayed as a man, and as the Mediator of his people; yet he spoke with majesty and authority, as one with and equal to the Father.
q: Read verses 1–5 (Christ's prayer for himself). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 6–10 (His prayer for his disciples), what do you learn about family and generations?
Verse 3 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 John 5:20. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of prayer in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us endeavour to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, praying that all believers may be more and more united in one mind and one judgment.
ch.a: Set aside a specific time this week to pray through this chapter's key verse.

bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.

It is supposed from the words of Nathanael in John 1:46 that the city of Nazareth was held in great disrepute, either because, it is said, the people of Galilee were a rude and less cultivated class, and were largely influenced by the Gentiles who mingled with them, or because of their lower type of moral and religious character. But there seems to be no sufficient reason for these suppositions.
The black torrent, the brook flowing through the ravine below the eastern wall of Jerusalem (John 18:1). (See KIDRON.)
Originally called Simon (=Simeon, i.e., "hearing"), a very common Jewish name in the New Testament. He was the son of Jona (Matt. 16:17).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ taken in the garden (vv. 1–12); Christ before Annas and Caiaphas (vv. 13–27); Christ before Pilate (vv. 28–40). People named: Peter, Pilate, Judas, Simon, Annas, Barabbas. Places: Nazareth, Cedron.
ch.mh: Sin began in the garden of Eden, there the curse was pronounced, there the Redeemer was promised; and in a garden that promised Seed entered into conflict with the old serpent.
q: Read verses 1–12 (Christ taken in the garden). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 13–27 (Christ before Annas and Caiaphas), what do you learn about discipleship?
Verse 37 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 John 4:6. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Peter’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of leadership and kingship in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us endeavour to make our accusers ashamed as Christ did; and let us beware of crucifying Christ afresh.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.

bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.

A "city of the Jews" (Luke 23:51), the birth-place of Joseph in whose sepulchre our Lord was laid (Matt. 27:57, 60; John 19:38). It is probably the same place as Ramathaim in Ephraim, and the birth-place of Samuel (1 Sam. 1:1, 19).
After the commencement of our Lord's public ministry little notice is taken of Mary. She was present at the marriage in Cana.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ condemned and crucified (vv. 1–18); Christ on the cross (vv. 19–30); His side pierced (vv. 31–37); The burial of Jesus (vv. 38–42). People named: Pilate, Cesar, Mary, Gabbatha, Golgotha, Cleophas. Places: Arimathea.
ch.mh: Little did Pilate think with what holy regard these sufferings of Christ would, in after-ages, be thought upon and spoken of by the best and greatest of men.
q: Read verses 1–18 (Christ condemned and crucified). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 19–30 (Christ on the cross), what do you learn about leadership and kingship?
Verse 30 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside John 17:4. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Pilate’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We must do our duty as the present day and opportunity are, and leave it to God to fulfil his promises in his own way and his own time.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.

o: The sepulchre found to be empty.
bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.
Twin, one of the twelve (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18, etc.). He was also called Didymus (John 11:16; 20:24), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name.

Mary Magdalene, i.e., Mary of Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Lake of Tiberias. She is for the first time noticed in Luke 8:3 as one of the women who "ministered to Christ of their substance."
Originally called Simon (=Simeon, i.e., "hearing"), a very common Jewish name in the New Testament. He was the son of Jona (Matt. 16:17).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The sepulchre found to be empty (vv. 1–10); Christ appears to Mary (vv. 11–18); He appears to the disciples (vv. 19–25); The unbelief of Thomas (vv. 26–29); Conclusion (vv. 30,31). People named: Thomas, Mary, Peter, Magdalene, Simon, Didymus.
ch.mh: If Christ gave his life a ransom, and had not taken it again, it would not have appeared that his giving it was accepted as satisfaction.
q: Read verses 1–10 (The sepulchre found to be empty). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 11–18 (Christ appears to Mary), what do you learn about discipleship?
Verse 31 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Acts 10:43. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Thomas’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of faith and trust in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We must do our best, and neither envy those who can do better, nor despise those who do as well as they can, though they come behind.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

bg: The genuineness of this Gospel, i.e., the fact that the apostle John was its author, is beyond all reasonable doubt. In recent times, from about 1820, many attempts have been made to impugn its genuineness, but without success.
Reedy, a town of Galilee, near Capernaum. Here our Lord wrought his first miracle, the turning of water into wine (John 2:1-11; 4:46).

When the Sanhedrin were about to proceed with some plan for the condemnation of our Lord (John 7:45-52), Nicodemus interposed in his behalf. (Comp. Deut. 1:16, 17; 17:8.) They replied, "Art thou also of Galilee?.... Out of Galilee ariseth no prophet."
Originally called Simon (=Simeon, i.e., "hearing"), a very common Jewish name in the New Testament. He was the son of Jona (Matt. 16:17).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Christ appears to his disciples (vv. 1–14); His discourse with Peter (vv. 15–19); Christ's declaration concerning John (vv. 20–24); The conclusion (vv. 25). People named: Peter, Simon, Tiberias, Thomas, Didymus, Nathanael. Places: Cana, Galilee, No.
ch.mh: Christ makes himself known to his people, usually in his ordinances; but sometimes by his Spirit he visits them when employed in their business.
q: Read verses 1–14 (Christ appears to his disciples). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 15–19 (His discourse with Peter), what do you learn about discipleship?
Verse 15 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 John 4:19. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Peter’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of love in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of John?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We may, however, look forward to the joy we shall receive in heaven, from a more complete knowledge of all Jesus did and said, as well as of the conduct of his providence and grace in his dealings with each of us.
ch.a: Do one concrete, unannounced act of love for someone in your home or church.
